```{python}
#| label: d4-setup
#| code-summary: "Chapter setup"
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from mdmx import artifacts, data, latex, plotting, provenance
from mdmx.config import params

provenance.start_chapter("d4-events")
plotting.use_style()
P = params()

names = dict(zip(pops["code"], pops["name"]))
```

## Why exceptional years are set aside

Wars and pandemics produce short, sharp mortality shocks with their own
age–sex signatures.  The Tucker decomposition is meant to describe the
*baseline* mortality surface — the slow secular transition — so the years
in which a population was hit by such an event are removed from the data
the decomposition sees, and kept aside for the disruption model of paper §6
(chapter 08).  A country-year is exceptional if, and only if, it appears in
the event dictionary.

## The event dictionary

The dictionary is a plain table, `config/events.csv`, with one row per event
and group of populations: the event, its type, first and last calendar
year, the HMD population codes affected, and a source.  `ALL` means every
population with data during the event (used for the influenza pandemics of
1957–58 and 1968–69 and for COVID-19).  Keeping the dictionary as data,
rather than as code, means the same file drives both the masks used in the
analysis and the dictionary's tables at the end of this chapter, so the two can never
disagree.

```{python}
#| label: d4-dictionary
#| code-summary: "Load and display the dictionary"
events = data.load_events()
artifacts.save("events", events, desc="Event dictionary (config/events.csv)")
with pd.option_context("display.max_colwidth", 60, "display.max_rows", 80):
    display(events[["id", "event", "type", "start", "end", "populations", "note"]])
```

### How the dictionary is compiled

Four choices shape the dictionary; where an entry needs a reason, the
`note` column above gives it.

* **The United Kingdom (GBR_NP) is listed with its parts.**  It is a
  population in its own right (chapter d1), so every war entry that lists
  England & Wales, Scotland or Northern Ireland lists it too.  Otherwise its
  war years, 1939–45 for example, would count as normal years while those
  of its parts are masked.
* **Entry dates.**  Each belligerent is flagged from the year it entered
  the war, so that its years before entry stay in the baseline: Italy and
  Bulgaria in World War I from 1915, the United States and Greece from
  1917; Italy and Greece in World War II from 1940 (the same entry lists
  Hungary and Bulgaria, which entered in 1941; their HMD series begin after
  the war), the United States from 1942; France and Britain in the Crimean
  War from 1854 and Sardinia (Italy) from 1855.  Two entries start earlier
  for some of the populations they list: World War II from 1939 for every
  population of its main entry, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg,
  Denmark and Norway (invaded in 1940) included, and the Napoleonic Wars
  from 1803 for Sweden, at war from 1805.  The populations that sent forces
  to the Second Boer War and the Korean War are flagged for those wars too,
  though little excess mortality is expected at home.
* **Sweden in the Seven Years' War** is flagged for 1757–1762, the years of
  its own (Pomeranian) war within the war of 1756–1763.
* **A fourth type, "other"**, records four mortality crises that are
  neither wars nor the three pandemic types: the Swedish famine and
  dysentery epidemic of 1772–73 (the lowest life expectancy in the HMD),
  the Icelandic measles epidemics of 1846 and 1882, and the 1871 smallpox
  epidemic in the Netherlands and Belgium.  These years are excluded from
  the baseline like other exceptional years, but they are too few and too
  heterogeneous to estimate a disruption profile, so the disruption model
  does not use them.

## Labelling every country-year

Each curated country-year receives a label $d_{c,t}$: 0 = none, 1 = war,
2 = respiratory pandemic, 3 = enteric pandemic, 4 = other.  When a
country-year is in more than one entry the label is chosen by priority
war > respiratory > enteric > other (paper §2.3): in 1918, for example, a
belligerent is labelled *war*.  All matching entries are kept in the
`all_events` column for transparency.

```{python}
#| label: d4-label
#| code-summary: "Expand the dictionary and label every curated country-year (cached)"
def _label():
    coverage = (lt_cur.groupby("pop")["year"].agg(["min", "max"])
                .rename(columns={"min": "first", "max": "last"}).reset_index())
    expanded = data.expand_events(events, coverage)
    country_years = lt_cur[["pop", "year"]].drop_duplicates().sort_values(["pop", "year"])
    return data.label_country_years(country_years, expanded)

labels = artifacts.stage("event_labels", _label, inputs=["lt_curated", "events"],
                         code=[_label, data.expand_events, data.label_country_years],
                         desc="Disruption label d(c,t) for every curated country-year")
counts = labels["type"].value_counts().reindex(list(data.LABELS.values()))
print(counts.to_string())
for lab, word in data.LABELS.items():
    key = "dataNLabel" + word.title()
    latex.report(key, int((labels["label"] == lab).sum()), desc=f"Country-years labelled {word}")
latex.report("dataNExceptional", int((labels["label"] > 0).sum()), desc="Exceptional country-years (all types)")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-s2-events
#| fig-cap: "Exceptional country-years in the HMD, by type. Each coloured cell is a country-year flagged by the event dictionary; light grey marks the other years with data."
#| fig-height: 7
TYPES = ["war", "respiratory", "enteric", "other"]
order = labels.groupby("pop")["year"].min().sort_values().index
years = np.arange(labels["year"].min(), labels["year"].max() + 1)
grid = np.full((len(order), len(years)), np.nan)
row = {p: i for i, p in enumerate(order)}
grid[labels["pop"].map(row), labels["year"] - years[0]] = labels["label"]
cmap = plt.matplotlib.colors.ListedColormap(["#e6e6e6"] + [plotting.COLORS[t] for t in TYPES])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 7))
ax.imshow(np.ma.masked_invalid(grid), aspect="auto", interpolation="nearest", cmap=cmap,
          vmin=-0.5, vmax=4.5, extent=(years[0] - 0.5, years[-1] + 0.5, len(order) - 0.5, -0.5))
ax.set_yticks(range(len(order)), [names[p] for p in order], fontsize=7)
ax.set_xlabel("Year"); ax.grid(False)
handles = [plt.matplotlib.patches.Patch(color=plotting.COLORS[t], label=t.title()) for t in TYPES]
ax.legend(handles=handles, loc="lower left", fontsize=8, frameon=True)
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s2-events")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-s2-events-e0
#| fig-cap: "Life expectancy at birth for six populations, female (red) and male (blue) lines, with exceptional years marked by type. The flagged years coincide with the visible dips."
SHOW = ["FRATNP", "GBRTENW", "SWE", "ITA", "USA", "JPN"]
e0 = lt_cur[lt_cur["age"] == 0].merge(labels[["pop", "year", "label"]], on=["pop", "year"])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(11, 6), sharey=True)
for ax, pop in zip(axes.flat, SHOW):
    for sex in data.SEXES:
        s = e0[(e0["pop"] == pop) & (e0["sex"] == sex)].sort_values("year")
        ax.plot(s["year"], s["ex"], color=plotting.COLORS[sex], lw=0.8)
        for lab, t in enumerate(TYPES, start=1):
            hit = s[s["label"] == lab]
            ax.scatter(hit["year"], hit["ex"], s=8, color=plotting.COLORS[t], zorder=3,
                       label=t.title() if (pop == SHOW[0] and sex == "female") else None)
    ax.set_title(names[pop], fontsize=10)
axes[0, 0].legend(fontsize=7)
for ax in axes[:, 0]:
    ax.set_ylabel(r"$e_0$")
plotting.save_figure(fig, "fig-s2-events-e0")
plt.show()
```

## A screen for crises the dictionary might miss

The dictionary is compiled from historical sources, so it can miss events.
As a check, the code below lists every *unlabelled* country-year whose
life expectancy (average of the sexes) falls more than
`{python} P.data.crisis_screen_drop` years below the median of the same population's
surrounding ±`{python} P.data.crisis_screen_halfwidth` years.  This is a **diagnostic
only** — nothing is changed automatically.  The four "other" crises were
identified this way and confirmed against historical sources.  The
country-years still listed below remain in the baseline: most are in the
very small Icelandic population, where single-year life expectancy is
volatile, and the rest are isolated dips without an established cause in
the sources used for the dictionary.
They are listed so that any reader can judge them.

```{python}
#| label: d4-screen
#| code-summary: "List unlabelled years with unusually low e0"
e0avg = (lt_cur[lt_cur["age"] == 0].groupby(["pop", "year"], as_index=False)["ex"].mean()
         .rename(columns={"ex": "e0"}))
screen = data.crisis_screen(e0avg, labels, drop=P.data.crisis_screen_drop,
                            halfwidth=P.data.crisis_screen_halfwidth)
artifacts.save("crisis_screen", screen, inputs=["lt_curated", "event_labels"],
               params=P.section("data"), desc="Unlabelled country-years with unusually low e0")
screen.assign(name=screen["pop"].map(names)).round(1)
```

## Appendix tables for the paper

Four tables list the dictionary, one per type; the article does not show them.  They are
generated from the same CSV file used above.

```{python}
#| label: d4-appendix
#| code-summary: "Write the appendix tables (one per type)"
TITLES = {"war": "War event dictionary", "respiratory": "Respiratory pandemic dictionary",
          "enteric": "Enteric pandemic dictionary", "other": "Other mortality crises"}
def _pop_list(cell):
    # A wrapped list breaks only between populations: the spaces inside a name are non-breaking.
    if cell.strip() == "ALL":
        return "All populations with data in these years"
    return ", ".join(n.replace(" ", "\u00a0") for n in dict.fromkeys(names.get(c, c) for c in cell.split()))
for t in TYPES:
    sub = events[events["type"] == t]
    tab = pd.DataFrame({
        "Event": sub["event"],
        "Years": [f"{a}" if a == b else f"{a}--{b}" for a, b in zip(sub["start"], sub["end"])],
        "HMD populations": [_pop_list(c) for c in sub["populations"]],
    })
    latex.save_table(tab, f"tbl-app-{t}", f"{TITLES[t]}.  Generated from \\texttt{{config/events.csv}}.",
                     column_format=(r">{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{4.2cm}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{1.6cm}"
                                    r">{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{\dimexpr\textwidth-6.2cm-4\tabcolsep\relax}"),
                     long=True)
```
